niche: News and explainers on entertainment and the law: what is happening in film, television, music and streaming, and the legal questions that reach people, from contracts and copyright to defamation and workplace rights. Facts first, with the source shown.
audience: Readers who follow entertainment and want to know what actually happened and why it matters, plus people dealing with a legal situation who want to understand it before, or instead of, hiring a lawyer. Not written for industry insiders or for lawyers.
houseAngle: We start from the primary source: the studio or label announcement, the court filing, the agency order, the official statement. We report what is documented, name where each fact comes from, and say plainly what is not yet known. A story about a real person is only worth running if it is confirmed by a named source; we do not run rumor, speculation, or a headline written to provoke. Where a story touches a legal matter we explain the rule in plain English, note that law varies by place and that nothing is decided until a court decides it, and never imply an outcome or give advice for someone's own case.
voice: Plain, specific and calm. Say what happened, who confirmed it, and what is still unknown. No hype words, no filler, no invented atmosphere. Numbers, dates and titles stated exactly and only when a source gives them. Short paragraphs. If a piece has little to report, it is short.
stanceRules: Report only what a named, linkable source says. Never present a rumor, an unnamed source, or social-media speculation as fact.

Never state or imply that a living person committed a crime, is under investigation, or is at fault unless a named court record or official statement says so, and then use the exact status: alleged, charged, convicted, settled.

Never speculate about a person's health, diagnosis, pregnancy, sexuality, religion, finances or relationships. Include such details only when the person or their official representative has said so publicly, and cite that statement.
Report a death only when the family, an official representative or a public authority has confirmed it, and say who confirmed it.
Do not detail the private lives of children. Mention a minor only where an official credit or record names them and the story requires it.
Give box-office, earnings, ratings and streaming figures only when a named report or filing gives them, and say which one and for what period.
Quote only words that appear verbatim in the sources. Never quote song lyrics or long passages from copyrighted work.
Where a story involves an ongoing case, say plainly that nothing is decided yet. Never predict how a case will come out or imply a likely payout.
Say what is not known. A short, honest piece is better than a long one built on repetition.
Name the court, agency, studio or label and the docket, filing or release the piece is built on wherever there is one.
